notes.meaning: Rehoboam stayed faithful to God during his first three years while his throne felt insecure. Once his power felt firm and settled, he abandoned God's law and led the whole nation into idolatry. It is an easy trap to seek God in hard times but walk away from Him as soon as life feels safe.

In Rehoboam's fifth year, King Shishak of Egypt marched against Jerusalem because Judah had broken faith with the Lord. Shishak had his own political ambitions, but Scripture explains that God used this foreign king to discipline His straying people. When people turn from God, He often uses difficult circumstances to awaken them to their sin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern historians identify Shishak as Pharaoh Sheshonq I, whose temple carvings at Karnak record his military campaign in the region around 925 BC.

notes.meaning: Shishak invaded with a vast force of twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen, and countless foot soldiers from Egypt and neighboring African lands. These troops included Libyans, Sukkites, and Cushites from south of Egypt. No human strength or army of Judah could stand against a force so overwhelming without the Lord's help.

The Egyptian army rapidly captured the fortified cities that Rehoboam had spent years building and strengthening. The quick collapse of these strongholds showed Judah that thick stone walls cannot protect people who have abandoned God. Soon the invaders were marching directly toward Jerusalem.

The prophet Shemaiah came to the king and his leaders while they were huddled in Jerusalem planning their defense. He gave them God's direct message: because they had abandoned the Lord, the Lord had abandoned them to Shishak. True safety always depends on our obedience to God, not on human schemes or military power.

Instead of making excuses, the king and his rulers bowed down and agreed that the Lord was righteous in judging them. They admitted that they had brought this calamity on themselves and that God's punishment was completely just. True repentance begins when we stop defending ourselves and agree with God's verdict on our sin.

When the Lord saw their sincere humility, He sent Shemaiah back with a promise of mercy. God promised He would not wipe Jerusalem out, but would give them partial relief and hold back His total wrath. God is always ready to show compassion the moment people humble their hearts before Him.

Although God spared Jerusalem from destruction, He allowed Shishak to make Judah a servant state that paid heavy taxes. This painful experience was meant to teach the people how light and good God's rule was compared to the harsh yoke of a foreign king. Serving the Lord brings true freedom, while rebelling against Him brings miserable slavery.

Shishak entered Jerusalem and stripped all the treasures from the temple of the Lord and the royal palace. He took everything valuable, including the magnificent gold shields King Solomon had made for his royal guard. Sin always costs far more than people expect, stripping away the spiritual and material blessings God had provided.

To replace the stolen gold shields, Rehoboam had cheaper bronze shields made and put them under the care of the palace guards. Whenever the king walked to the temple, the guards carried these imitation shields and then locked them away in the guardroom out of sight. This showed how quickly Judah's glory had fallen, settling for a cheap substitute while trying to maintain outward appearances.

Because Rehoboam humbled himself, God turned His anger away and decided not to wipe out the kingdom. In addition, faithful people and good deeds were still found across Judah, which gave hope for the future. Even when things look dark, God notices and honors those who still remain faithful to Him.

After the Egyptian crisis passed, Rehoboam regained strength and continued his seventeen-year reign in Jerusalem. The writer emphasizes that Jerusalem was the special city chosen by God for His worship, making the king's unfaithfulness even more tragic. The verse also mentions that his mother was an Ammonite foreigner, which likely pushed him toward idol worship in his youth.

The Bible summarizes Rehoboam's life by stating that he did evil because he never set his heart to seek the Lord. He never firmly committed himself to God, so his good moments were brief and easily faded away. A divided heart will always drift into compromise and spiritual failure.

The complete history of Rehoboam's reign was preserved in the writings of the prophets Shemaiah and Iddo, books that are no longer available today. His entire rule was marked by ongoing skirmishes and border wars against King Jeroboam of the northern tribes. Turning away from God leaves behind a legacy of division and strife.

Rehoboam died and was buried with his royal ancestors in the City of David, and his son Abijah succeeded him as king. Despite Rehoboam's many failures and weak faith, God kept His covenant promise to preserve David's royal line. God remains faithful to His promises even when human leaders fail.
